chapter_theme: The mullai section of the Kainnilai (25-36, Pullankadanar), much of it lost in the manuscripts: in the rains the friend shows the waiting heroine the mullai's teeth, the red thonri, the stag with his doe and the plumed horses he will yoke as proof he will come; the heroine's evening, with the cowherds entering the common and blowing their pipes, brings pallor; in 34 he has come.

25.reading: The friend tells the heroine of wide sword-bright eyes that in the woodland the rains have made, the creeping mullai has grown lovely and put out sharp teeth as its shoots bud, so their lover will surely come: let her not take on this grieving, pallid sickness.
25.nuance: The buds are the creeper's teeth, so the woodland already smiles; the friend's argument is that the season has kept its side of the promise and the sickness (பைதல்நோய்) has no ground left. ஓரும் is an expletive of assurance, not a verb.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-made woodland and the mullai in bud

comparisons.tenor: the pointed white mullai buds, as sharp teeth
the heroine's eyes, bright and long as a sword

26.reading: The friend tells the heroine of gold-like colour that, now the blood-red thonri puts out its sharp buds, so red that a bird climbing the pidavam shies from them as from blazing fire, it is unlikely he will fail to come.
26.nuance: Line 2 opens with a gap, so who takes the buds for what is partly guessed: சேவல் என may mean the creature takes the red bud for a cock's comb before shying from it as fire. அரிது ... வாரா விடல் is a double negative: his not coming is the hard thing.

thinai_evidence.note: the thonri and pidavam bloom in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the thonri flower, red as blood
the red thonri buds, which a bird shies from as from fire

27.reading: In the evening the rains bring, when something now lost comes in swaying, pallor spreads over her body as she thinks of the coming of the man who was one with her.
27.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are lost but for ஒல்கப் புகுதரு, perhaps the herds or the cloud entering at dusk. The pallor rises from thinking of his coming (வரவுள்ளி), not of his going: expectation, not only absence, feeds it.

28.reading: In the woodland where the rain has poured, the friend says, their lover, if he saw these signs, would drive his chariot of swift horses back without delay; the rest is lost.
28.nuance: இவர் is read as 'these' (the season's signs) rather than a person; with lines 1 and 4 lost, the conditional (if he saw) could also be a reproach that he has not seen them.

29.reading: A fragment: the kurunthu blooms, the proud stag embraces his doe, and the rain-cloud comes over the forest and thunders; how the scene was applied to the lovers is lost.
29.nuance: The stag embracing his doe is the classic iraicchi carrier of mullai, but with the closing lines lost the deletion test cannot be run, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: kurunthu in bloom and the rain-cloud

30.reading: A fragment: only the time survives, the hour when the cowherds who have blown their konrai pipes come into the village common.
30.nuance: The pipe is made of the konrai pod (கொன்றை ... குழல்), the herders' own instrument; what was said to happen at that hour is lost with lines 1 and 2.

31.reading: A fragment: only the end survives, seeing the cloud come and give its drops.
31.nuance: Three of four lines are lost; the speaker and the sense of 'having seen' cannot be fixed.

32.reading: A fragment: with the sky meeting the rains and swift fire of lightning, she asks her own heart whether it will not tell the sign set for the evening of piercing fire.
32.nuance: The address to the heart (நெஞ்சே) survives but its first word is broken (மெழு); a returning hero urging his heart on would also fit. The evening called sharp fire repeats the lightning's fire of line 1, as if the evening itself burns.

comparisons.tenor: the evening, piercing as sharp fire

33.reading: The friend tells the heroine, as the buds loosen their bonds, that he will come yoking his fine, spirited, plumed horses: will he not take away the sickness she has suffered?
33.nuance: Only the promise and its question survive; the horses' plumes (உளை) belong to the chariot of return, and the question form makes the cure his to bring, not hers to find.

34.reading: As the mullai put out its teeth and the clouds, having scooped the sea, pour their rain, the lover has come; the rest, about their being joined, is broken.
34.nuance: Unlike its neighbours the verse reports the arrival as done (வந்தார்), so the season's signs are here a fulfilment, not a promise.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai in bud and the rains pouring

35.reading: A fragment: at the hour when the herders, milk on their lips and heedless of others' grief, blow their sweet pipes, something is hard to bear.
35.nuance: தெரிவிலர், they do not know, makes the herders innocent of the pain they cause; the pipe is sweet, and the torment is in her hearing it at that hour. பால்வாய் is read as milk-mouthed, the herders fresh from the milking; the last line breaks off at அரித.

36.reading: The friend tells the heroine wearing a garland of large flowers that, now the pidavam, kurunthu and asoka bloom, the young peacock calls and the monkeys shiver in the cold, he will not stay away: he will come, taking this as his sign.
36.nuance: இடபம் in the last line is obscure: read as the sign or token (perhaps the zodiac bull marking the season's turn); the close turns on it. The female monkey belongs to the hills, a kurinji thing in a mullai catalogue.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season blossoms of the woodland

links.note: Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man says the mullai buds along the road stand sharp like the teeth of his simple girl (முள்ளெயிறு ஏய்ப்ப). Kainnilai 25: the friend shows the heroine the mullai putting out sharp teeth (கூர்எயிறு ஈன) as proof he will come.
links.teaches: One bud is read at both ends of the waiting: on the road the man sees her teeth in it, at home the friend offers it to her as his promise kept, so the mullai's teeth tie the two absent lovers to a single sight.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 26: the thondri blooms over every field like the first-night lamps of Karthigai, and the rain comes as messenger. Kainnilai 26: the blood-red thonri buds are so like fire that a bird shies from them.
links.teaches: Both friends read the red thonri as flame, but one sees festival lamps and the other a fire that frightens, so the same sign of return can carry welcome or alarm, and the Kainnilai friend lets a trace of fear into her comfort.

links.note: Kural 1182: the woman says pallor rides over her body (மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு), claiming it is his gift. Kainnilai 27: at the rainy evening, thinking of his coming, pallor spreads over her body (ஊர்தரு மேனி பசப்பு).
links.teaches: The couplet says only that pallor rides her body by his right; the Kainnilai fragment gives it an hour and a cause, the rain-season evening and the thought of his coming, so expectation, not only absence, is what sets the pallor moving.

links.note: Akananuru 23: in the rains the stag embraces his doe (பிணை ... தழீஇ), and the woman asks if this is the time her man meant. Kainnilai 29: kurunthu blooms, the stag embraces his doe and the rain-cloud thunders; the rest is lost.
links.teaches: The Akananuru poem shows the stag's embrace being weighed as the promised season's clock, which tells a reader of the broken Kainnilai verse what such an embrace was there to measure, even though its own ending is gone.

links.note: Akananuru 14: the wife asks what will become of them by morning if he does not remember even in the evening when the cattle crowd into the common (மன்றுநிறை புகுதரும் மாலையும்). Kainnilai 30: the hour when the cowherds with konrai pipes enter the common (மன்றம் புகுதரும் போழ்து).
links.teaches: The Akananuru wife names the homecoming to the common as the hour by which a man who remembers would be back, which explains why the Kainnilai poet could mark the waiting by that hour alone: the village's return is the measure of his not returning.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 22: the returning man says the plumed, spirited horses are yoked (உளையணிந்து ... கலிமாவும் பூட்டிய). Kainnilai 33: the friend says he will come yoking his fine spirited plumed horses (உளையார் கலிநன் மாப்பூட்டி வருவார்).
links.teaches: The friend's promise uses nearly the words with which the hero himself reports setting out, so the comfort at home is shown to be an accurate picture of what is happening on the road, and the formula passes between the friend's and the hero's mouths.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 33: the man says he set as his sign the time when the cloud that drew up the sea (கடனீர் முகந்த) would gather on the western hill. Kainnilai 34: as the cloud that scooped the sea pours (கடல்முகந்து கார்பொழிய), the lover has come.
links.teaches: Held together, the two verses close the loop of the mullai promise: one poet's hero names the sea-drinking cloud as his appointed sign, and the other poet has the lover arrive exactly as that cloud breaks.

links.note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could bear the friend's comfort but for the harsh small pipe the unlettered cowherds blow (கல்லாக் கோவலர் ஊதும் வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) at evening. Kainnilai 35: the herders who do not know (தெரிவிலர்) blow the sweet pipe (தீங்குழல்).
links.teaches: Both poets excuse the herders by their ignorance, but one calls the pipe harsh and the other sweet, which shows that the cruelty is not in the sound itself but in the hour and the ear that hears it.

links.note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute is the messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Kainnilai 35: the herders, heedless, blow the sweet pipe at that hour.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the flute a weapon; the Kainnilai adds that those who wield it do not know they are wounding anyone, so the evening's weapon kills without a killer who intends it.

source_issues: Kainnilai 26-35 are damaged in the source: 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32 and 35 have whole lines with no Tamil letters, and 26, 33, 34 and 35 have broken lines; readings cover only what survives and every damaged verse is marked uncertain.
Kainnilai 32 line 3: 'லக மெழுநெஞ்சே' begins mid-word; the vocative may be 'எழு நெஞ்சே' (rise, heart), which would change the speaker.
Kainnilai 35: the site's text lacks lines 1 and 2 (flag site_diff); line 4 ends after அரித.
Kainnilai 36 line 4: இடபம் is obscure in sense.
